prompt:

A pair of actions is a *Nash equilibrium* if neither player can get a strictly higher payoff by changing only their own action. A pair of actions is a *pair of mutual best responses* if each player's action gives them a maximal payoff against the other player's action.

*Circling best responses* in a payoff matrix means: (1) in every column, circle Player 1's maximum payoff in that column (all maxima if tied); (2) in every row, circle Player 2's maximum payoff in that row; (3) a cell with both payoffs circled is a mutual best response.

Prove that the process of circling best responses finds exactly all (pure strategy) Nash equilibria.
answer: A profile is a Nash equilibrium iff both of its payoffs are circled (each player's payoff is maximal among their own deviations).

solutions.title: Unpack both definitions
solutions.body:
Fix a profile $(a_1,a_2)$.

Player 1 has no profitable deviation iff $u_1(a_1,a_2)\ge u_1(a_1',a_2)$ for every row $a_1'$, i.e. iff $u_1(a_1,a_2)$ is a maximum of its column, i.e. iff Player 1's payoff in this cell is circled.

Similarly Player 2 has no profitable deviation iff $u_2(a_1,a_2)\ge u_2(a_1,a_2')$ for every column $a_2'$, iff Player 2's payoff in this cell is circled.

So $(a_1,a_2)$ is a Nash equilibrium iff neither player has a profitable deviation iff both payoffs in its cell are circled. Hence the doubly circled cells are exactly the pure Nash equilibria. $\blacksquare$

Does every extensive form game with a finite number of moves have at least one Subgame Perfect Nash Equilibrium? Justify your answer.

solutions.title: Induction on the length of the longest path
solutions.body:
**Yes.** We prove by induction on $n$, the number of moves in the longest path of the tree, that every such game has an SPE.

*Base case $n=1$.* Only one decision node (the root) with terminal children: the player who moves picks an action with the largest payoff for themselves. This is a Nash equilibrium of the game, and the only subgame is the game itself, so it is an SPE.

*Inductive step.* Suppose every game whose longest path has at most $n$ moves has an SPE, and take a game $G$ whose longest path has $n+1$ moves. Call a decision node *last* if all its children are terminal. The subgame at a last node is a one-move game: the mover picks an action with the largest payoff for themselves (ties broken arbitrarily). Fix such a choice $\sigma_\ell$ at every last node $\ell$, and let $G'$ be the game obtained by replacing each last node $\ell$ by a terminal node with the payoffs of the chosen action. The longest path of $G'$ has at most $n$ moves, so $G'$ has an SPE $\sigma'$. Let $\sigma$ be $\sigma'$ together with the choices $\sigma_\ell$.

We claim $\sigma$ is an SPE of $G$. At a last node this is true by construction. Let $d$ be any other decision node and suppose a player $i$ deviates in the subgame $G_d$ to a strategy $\tau$. Modify $\tau$ at the last nodes where $i$ moves, replacing it with $\sigma_\ell$; this does not decrease $i$'s payoff, because $\sigma_\ell$ is a best action for the mover at $\ell$ given what follows. The modified deviation is a deviation in the subgame $G'_d$ of $G'$ (with last nodes replaced by their payoffs), where $\sigma'$ is a Nash equilibrium, so it is not profitable. Hence the original deviation was not profitable either, and $\sigma$ is a Nash equilibrium of every subgame of $G$. $\blacksquare$

answer: Label the squares by the Lo Shu magic square; the $8$ winning lines are exactly the $8$ triples of distinct numbers in $\{1,\dots,9\}$ with sum $15$.

solutions.title: Use the magic square
solutions.body:
Label the nine squares with the numbers of the magic square
$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|}\hline 2&7&6\\\hline 9&5&1\\\hline 4&3&8\\\hline\end{array}$$
This is a bijection between squares and the numbers $1,\dots,9$. Every row, column and long diagonal of the grid sums to $15$, so each of the $8$ winning lines is a triple of distinct numbers with sum $15$.

Conversely, the triples of distinct numbers from $\{1,\dots,9\}$ with sum $15$ are exactly $\{1,5,9\},\{1,6,8\},\{2,4,9\},\{2,5,8\},\{2,6,7\},\{3,4,8\},\{3,5,7\},\{4,5,6\}$. These are the $8$ lines of the grid: rows $\{2,7,6\},\{9,5,1\},\{4,3,8\}$, columns $\{2,9,4\},\{7,5,3\},\{6,1,8\}$, diagonals $\{2,5,8\},\{6,5,4\}$.

So under the bijection square $\leftrightarrow$ number, a set of squares contains a winning line iff the corresponding set of numbers contains a triple with sum $15$. The two games have the same turn order, the same winning conditions and the same tie condition, and the correspondence maps every position (set of chosen squares for each player) to the corresponding position and each legal move to the corresponding legal move. So it maps strategies to strategies bijectively (a strategy is a choice of move at every position of a player) and preserves the payoffs (win, tie, lose). Hence the games are equivalent. $\blacksquare$

prompt:
A normal form game $(N,\{A_i\},\{u_i\})$ is *equivalent* to an extensive form game with players $N$, strategy spaces $S_i$ and payoff functions $u_i'$ if for each player $i$ there is a bijection $h_i:A_i\to S_i$ such that $u(a_1,\dots,a_n)=u'(h_1(a_1),\dots,h_n(a_n))$ for every action profile. Likewise, an extensive form game is equivalent to a normal form game if there are bijections $g_i:S_i\to A_i$ with $u(s_1,\dots,s_n)=u'(g_1(s_1),\dots,g_n(s_n))$ for all strategy profiles.

Show that a normal form game is equivalent to an extensive form game if and only if the extensive form game is equivalent to the normal form game.

solutions.title: Invert the bijections
solutions.body:
($\Rightarrow$) Suppose the normal form game is equivalent to the extensive form game via bijections $h_i:A_i\to S_i$ with $u(a_1,\dots,a_n)=u'(h_1(a_1),\dots,h_n(a_n))$. Bijections have inverses, so define $g_i=h_i^{-1}:S_i\to A_i$, which is a bijection. For any strategy profile $(s_1,\dots,s_n)$, put $a_i=g_i(s_i)$, so $h_i(a_i)=s_i$; then $u'(s_1,\dots,s_n)=u'(h_1(a_1),\dots,h_n(a_n))=u(a_1,\dots,a_n)=u(g_1(s_1),\dots,g_n(s_n))$. That is exactly the definition of the extensive form game being equivalent to the normal form game.

($\Leftarrow$) The same argument with the roles reversed: given bijections $g_i$ satisfying the second condition, $h_i=g_i^{-1}$ satisfy the first. $\blacksquare$

solutions.title: Define the normal form from strategies
solutions.body: **Yes.** Given a two-player extensive form game with strategy spaces $S_1,S_2$ and payoffs $u_i(s_1,s_2)$ (the payoff at the terminal node reached when both players follow their strategies), define the normal form game with action sets $A_1=S_1$, $A_2=S_2$ and payoffs $u_i'(a_1,a_2)=u_i(a_1,a_2)$. solutions.title: Compare pure Nash equilibria
solutions.body:
**No.** Consider the *matching parity game*: each player chooses $1$ or $2$. If the numbers have the same parity, Player 1 gets $1$ and Player 2 gets $0$; otherwise Player 2 gets $1$ and Player 1 gets $0$.

This game has no pure Nash equilibrium: in a profile with equal parity Player 2 can deviate and get $1$ instead of $0$; in a profile with different parity Player 1 can deviate and get $1$ instead of $0$.

Suppose it were equivalent to some finite extensive form game. By Problem 1.10 (backward induction) the extensive game has a Subgame Perfect Nash Equilibrium, which by Problem 1.8 is a Nash equilibrium, in pure strategies. An equivalence is a payoff-preserving bijection of the strategy spaces, so it carries Nash equilibria to Nash equilibria. Then the matching parity game would have a pure Nash equilibrium, a contradiction. $\blacksquare$

When players play $p_1,p_2$ independently, Player 1's expected payoff is $U_1(p_1,p_2)=\sum_{x\in A_1}\sum_{y\in A_2}p_1(x)p_2(y)u_1(x,y)$, and similarly for $U_2$. In rock-paper-scissors (payoff $1$ for a win, $0$ for a draw, $-1$ for a loss), suppose player one plays rock, paper, and scissors each with probability $1/3$. Show that player two cannot get a strictly higher expected payoff than by also playing each with probability $1/3$.
answer: Every strategy of player two earns expected payoff $0$ against the uniform strategy.

solutions.title: Compute the expected payoff
solutions.body:
Against the uniform mixed strategy of player one, any pure move of player two wins with probability $\frac13$, draws with probability $\frac13$ and loses with probability $\frac13$, so its expected payoff is $\frac13\cdot1+\frac13\cdot0+\frac13\cdot(-1)=0$.

If player two plays rock, paper, scissors with probabilities $r,p,1-r-p$, the expected payoff is $r\cdot0+p\cdot0+(1-r-p)\cdot0=0$, independent of $r,p$. So no strategy gives player two more than $0$, which is what the uniform strategy gives. $\blacksquare$

$$U_1(\delta_a,p_{-1})=U_1(\delta_b,p_{-1})=U_1(p_1,p_{-1}).$$
answer: $U_1(p_1,p_{-1})$ is a weighted average of the numbers $U_1(\delta_x,p_{-1})$, each at most $U_1(p_1,p_{-1})$; so every term with positive weight equals it.

solutions.title: Weighted average argument
solutions.body:
Let $m=U_1(p_1,p_{-1})$. Since $p_1$ is a best response, no deviation to a point mass can do better: $U_1(\delta_x,p_{-1})\le m$ for every $x\in A_1$.

But $m=\sum_x p_1(x)U_1(\delta_x,p_{-1})$ with weights $p_1(x)\ge0$ summing to $1$. If some $x$ with $p_1(x)>0$ had $U_1(\delta_x,p_{-1})<m$, then, as all other terms are at most $m$, the weighted average would be strictly less than $m$, a contradiction. In the mixed strategy extension of a game, an action $a_i$ of player $i$ is *dominated* if for every mixed strategy $p_{-i}$ of the other players there is a mixed strategy $p_i$ with $U_i(p_i,p_{-i})>U_i(\delta_{a_i},p_{-i})$ (we then say $a_i$ is dominated by $p_i$).

Suppose action $a_i$ is dominated by some strategy $p_i$ such that $p_i(a_i)>0$ (action $a_i$ is played with positive probability in $p_i$). Show that $a_i$ is dominated by some strategy $p_i'$ such that $p_i'(a_i)=0$.

solutions.title: Renormalize
solutions.body:
Let $t=p_i(a_i)>0$. We cannot have $t=1$, since then $p_i=\delta_{a_i}$ and $U_i(p_i,\cdot)>U_i(\delta_{a_i},\cdot)$ would be absurd. Define $p_i'(x)=\frac{p_i(x)}{1-t}$ for $x\ne a_i$ and $p_i'(a_i)=0$. This is a probability distribution, and $p_i=t\,\delta_{a_i}+(1-t)\,p_i'$.

Fix any $p_{-i}$ for which $U_i(p_i,p_{-i})>U_i(\delta_{a_i},p_{-i})$. By linearity of $U_i$ in the player's own strategy,
$$U_i(p_i,p_{-i})=t\,U_i(\delta_{a_i},p_{-i})+(1-t)\,U_i(p_i',p_{-i}).$$
The inequality becomes $(1-t)U_i(p_i',p_{-i})>(1-t)U_i(\delta_{a_i},p_{-i})$, i.e. $U_i(p_i',p_{-i})>U_i(\delta_{a_i},p_{-i})$. So $p_i'$, which never plays $a_i$, does strictly better than $a_i$ against every such $p_{-i}$ (and it is the same $p_i'$ whenever the original $p_i$ was). $\blacksquare$

answer: Dominated actions are never in a best response (swap them out); non-dominated ones are a best response to some $p_{-i}$.

solutions.title: Both directions
solutions.body:
($\Rightarrow$) Let $a_i$ be dominated, and let $q_i$ be any mixed strategy with $q_i(a_i)=c>0$ and $p_{-i}$ any opponent strategy. Choose $p_i$ with $U_i(p_i,p_{-i})>U_i(\delta_{a_i},p_{-i})$. Let $q_i'=q_i-c\,\delta_{a_i}+c\,p_i$, which is a probability distribution (the weight $c$ on $a_i$ is moved to $p_i$). By linearity, $U_i(q_i',p_{-i})-U_i(q_i,p_{-i})=c\left(U_i(p_i,p_{-i})-U_i(\delta_{a_i},p_{-i})\right)>0$. So $q_i$ is not a best response to $p_{-i}$. Hence $a_i$ is never played with positive probability in a best response.

($\Leftarrow$) Suppose $a_i$ is not dominated. Then there is an opponent strategy $p_{-i}$ for which no $p_i$ satisfies $U_i(p_i,p_{-i})>U_i(\delta_{a_i},p_{-i})$, i.e. $U_i(\delta_{a_i},p_{-i})\ge U_i(p_i,p_{-i})$ for all $p_i$. So $\delta_{a_i}$, which plays $a_i$ with probability $1$, is a best response to $p_{-i}$. Thus $a_i$ is played with positive probability in some best response. By contraposition, if $a_i$ is never in any best response, it is dominated. $\blacksquare$

solutions.title: Explicit epsilon-delta
solutions.body:
Let $M=|v_{11}|+|v_{12}|+|v_{21}|+|v_{22}|$ and write $V=\sum w_{jk}(q_1,q_2)v_{jk}$ with the four weights $w_{11}=q_1q_2$, $w_{12}=q_1(1-q_2)$, $w_{21}=(1-q_1)q_2$, $w_{22}=(1-q_1)(1-q_2)$. Fix $q_2$. Expanding, $V(q_1,q_2)=q_1\,\alpha(q_2)+\beta(q_2)$ with $\alpha(q_2)=q_2v_{11}+(1-q_2)v_{12}-q_2v_{21}-(1-q_2)v_{22}$ and $\beta(q_2)=q_2v_{21}+(1-q_2)v_{22}$, constants with respect to $q_1$. Then $f(q_1)=\alpha q_1+\beta$ satisfies

You may use the following facts, where $X,Y$ are closed intervals and $f:X\times Y\to\mathbb R$ is continuous.

*Fact 1.* There exist $x_1,x_2\in X$ and $y_1,y_2\in Y$ such that $(x_1,y_1)$ solves $\max_x\min_y f(x,y)$ and $(x_2,y_2)$ solves $\min_y\max_x f(x,y)$.

*Fact 2 (Min-Max Theorem).* If moreover $f(x,\hat y)$ is convex in $x$ for each $\hat y$ and $f(\hat x,y)$ is concave in $y$ for each $\hat x$, then $\max_x\min_y f(x,y)=\min_y\max_x f(x,y)$.

solutions.title: Apply the facts
solutions.body:
By Problems 2.9, 2.11 and 2.12, $V$ is a continuous function on $[0,1]\times[0,1]$ that is convex in $q_1$ and concave in $q_2$. So the Min-Max Theorem gives $v:=\max_{q_1}\min_{q_2}V=\min_{q_2}\max_{q_1}V$.

By Fact 1 there is $q_1^*$ attaining the maximum in $\max_{q_1}\min_{q_2}V$ (so $\min_{q_2}V(q_1^*,q_2)=v$) and $q_2^*$ attaining the minimum in $\min_{q_2}\max_{q_1}V$ (so $\max_{q_1}V(q_1,q_2^*)=v$). Then

solutions.title: Check both players
solutions.body:
Let $v$ denote the common value, so $q_1^*$ is a maximizer of $q_1\mapsto\min_{q_2}V(q_1,q_2)$ and $q_2^*$ a minimizer of $q_2\mapsto\max_{q_1}V(q_1,q_2)$ (this is how they were chosen), with $V(q_1^*,q_2^*)=v$.

Describe a Nash equilibrium of the second price auction. Justify that it is a Nash equilibrium.

solutions.title: Truthful bidding
solutions.body:
Let every agent bid their value: $b_i=v_i$. The agent $w$ with the largest value wins and pays the second largest value, which is less than $v_w$ (values are distinct).

*The winner* has payoff $v_w-p\ge0$ with $p\le v_w$, so by Problem 3.3 has no profitable deviation.

*A loser $i$* has utility $0$. To win, they would have to bid more than the highest other bid, which is at least $v_w>v_i$, and then they would pay at least $v_w>v_i$, for a negative utility. So no deviation is profitable.

Hence bidding one's value is a Nash equilibrium. $\blacksquare$

Suppose $p(q)=22-2q$, $c_1(q_1)=6q_1$ and $c_2(q_2)=2q_2$. (The function $f(x)=-(x-a)(x-b)$ attains its maximum at $x=\frac{a+b}2$.)

solutions.title: Maximize a quadratic
solutions.body:

solutions.body:
Firm two observes $q_1$ and best responds with $q_2(q_1)=5-\frac{q_1}2$ (Problem 3.8). Firm one anticipates this: its profit is $\left(22-2\left(q_1+5-\frac{q_1}2\right)\right)q_1-6q_1=(12-q_1)q_1-6q_1=-q_1(q_1-6)$, maximized at $q_1=3$.

prompt:
*Ice cream on the beach.* All $500$ participants are at a beach that is $500$ meters long, one person at every meter. Ice cream stand A is at meter $0$ and stand B is at meter $500$. Stand A charges price $p_A$ and stand B charges price $p_B$. The overall cost of buying from a stand is its price plus the distance to the stand (so for someone at meter $50$ the cost from A is $50+p_A$ and from B is $450+p_B$). Each participant buys from the stand with the lower overall cost (if indifferent, they choose at random). Each stand's payoff is its price times the number of people it serves.

At what meter is the cost of going to stand A equal to the cost of going to stand B if stand A charges $p_A$ and stand B charges $p_B$?

solutions.title: Set the costs equal
solutions.body:
For someone at meter $d$: $p_A+d=p_B+(500-d)$, so $2d=p_B-p_A+500$ and $d=\frac{p_B-p_A+500}{2}$.

**Answer: $d=\frac{p_B-p_A+500}2$**

Everyone at meters below $d=\frac{p_B-p_A+500}{2}$ buys from A, so A serves $d$ people and B serves $500-d=\frac{p_A-p_B+500}2$ people. Hence

solutions.title: Redo the best-response computation
solutions.body:
The indifferent meter $d'$ solves $p_A+\frac{d'}2=p_B+\frac{500-d'}2$, so $d'=p_B-p_A+250$. Profits: $u_A=p_A(p_B-p_A+250)=-p_A\left(p_A-(250+p_B)\right)$ and $u_B=p_B(p_A-p_B+250)$. Best responses: $p_A=125+\frac{p_B}2$ and $p_B=125+\frac{p_A}2$. Equilibrium: $p_A=p_B=250$.

At these prices $d'=250$, so each stand again serves $250$ people (as before, where $d=250$ too). In the old equilibrium each stand earned $500\cdot250=125{,}000$; now each earns $250\cdot250=62{,}500$. The prices are lower and the numbers served are unchanged, so the stands make less money.

**Answer: $p_A=p_B=250$; they make less money**
